an1.248:1.1: Tapussa and Bhallika were merchants from Ukkalā (modern Odisha on the Bay of Bengal) who offered the first meal to the Buddha after his awakening ([pli-tv-kd1:4.2.1]()). Their spiritual attainments are noted at [an6.119]()–20 (which also features others in this list). Tapussa also appears at [an9.41]().
an1.249:1.1: His given name was Sudatta, but he is usually known by the sobriquet Anāthapiṇḍika, “feeder of the poor”. Renowned as the foremost of benefactors, Anāthapiṇḍika appears in over twenty discourses in the Saṁyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāyas, discussing matters such as generosity, guarding the mind, and the development of meditation. The story of his conversion is recorded in the Vinaya ([pli-tv-kd16:4.1.1]()). He is well known for his offering of the monastery at which the Buddha most often stayed. His death and return are recounted in [mn143]().
an1.250:1.1: The householder Citta of Macchikāsaṇḍa was a chief lay disciple ([an2.132:1.2]()). His boldness and intelligence mark his distinctive personality. Likely he was born under the asterism Citrā (the star Spica), a manifestation of Agni (see Pāṇini 4.3.34, _vārttika_ 1). The primordial myth of the asterism attributes to it the power to enable one of lower status (the titans) to challenge those of higher status, the gods (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 2.1.2.13–17). Citta the householder is likewise noted for his brilliant insight that surpasses the monks ([sn41.1]()); moreover, on several occasions in his presence the most junior monastic surpasses the senior (eg. [sn41.2]()).
an1.251:1.1: and managing a large following is featured in [an8.23]() and [an8.24](). He is often paired with Citta as exemplars of male lay followers (eg. [sn17.23:1.4]()), and he holds a discussion with the Buddha at [an3.35]().
an1.252:1.1: Mahānāma was the brother of Anuruddha and Ānanda ([pli-tv-kd17:1.1.3]()) which, according to the commentary, makes the Buddha his cousin. He remained in the lay life as a devoted and generous follower, keenly interested in developing his practice. The early texts do not record any occasion of his awakening. However, the commentarial claim that he was a once-returner is supported by passages such as [sn55.22:2.3]() and [sn55.21:3.6]() that suggest he was indeed a noble disciple.
an1.253:1.1: The Uggas were one of the leading _khattiya_ clans of Vesālī. Ugga’s giving is exemplified at [an5.44]().
an1.254:1.1: His name varies between Ugga and Uggata; I use Uggata for clarity. He is praised for eight qualities by the Buddha at [an8.22](), one of which is that when serving the Saṅgha he makes no distinction between different monastics. He converses with the Buddha at [sn35.125]().
an1.255:1.1: Of the same clan as Ambaṭṭha of [dn3](), he does not seem to be mentioned elsewhere.
an1.256:1.1: Jīvaka was the Buddha’s doctor. His story is told in [pli-tv-kd8](), where we learn that he was abandoned on a trash heap by his mother Sālavatī, only to be discovered and raised by Prince Abhaya of Magadha, a Jain ([mn58]()). He was called “Survivor” (_jīvaka_) and “Raised by a Prince” (_komārabhacca_). On one occasion, he discussed the ethics of eating meat with the Buddha ([mn55]()). In later Ayurveda, _kaumārabhṛtya_ means “paediatrics”, and a lost treatise on that subject is attributed to Jīvaka (Jīvakatantra).
an1.257:1.1: Nakula’s father and mother ([an1.266]()) were an ideal married couple who wanted to be together in this life and the next, and trusted each other implicitly ([an4.55]()). The father was counseled by the Buddha in a time of sickness ([sn22.1]()). He also recovered from a previous illness with the help of his wife ([an6.16]()). Each features independently in Suttas as well ([sn22.1](), [sn35.131](), [an8.48]()). Nothing is known of their son Nakula himself, nor are their personal names recorded.
